name: Podman
vendor: Podman Container Tools, a CNCF sandbox project; started and still mostly maintained by Red Hat
summary: Runs Docker-style containers without a daemon, as root or as an ordinary user, and hands long-running ones to systemd.
intro: Podman runs containers without a daemon. Each `podman` command does its job and exits: `podman run` prepares the container’s storage and network, then starts `conmon`, a small monitor process, which launches an OCI runtime (`crun` by default, or `runc`) to create the container. `conmon` stays behind to hold the container’s output streams, write its logs and record its exit code. The container is therefore a descendant of whatever started it, a shell or a systemd unit, not of a long-running server. Run by an ordinary user, Podman creates a user namespace mapped onto that user’s ranges in `/etc/subuid` and `/etc/subgid`, so root inside the container is your own account outside, and Podman itself never gains privileges. Rootful containers get bridge networks from Netavark, with container names served by the aardvark-dns DNS server; rootless ones get their network device from `pasta`. Containers can be grouped into pods that share network, IPC and hostname namespaces, matching Kubernetes defaults, and `podman kube play` runs Kubernetes Pod and Deployment YAML directly.

The command line copies Docker’s, so `alias docker=podman` works for most people, and `podman build` uses Buildah underneath. For tools that speak the Docker API, `podman system service` serves a Docker-compatible REST API, alongside Podman’s own, on a Unix socket that systemd starts on demand; `docker-compose` and the `podman compose` wrapper talk to it. For long-running services, Quadlet turns small `.container`, `.pod` or `.kube` files into systemd units, and `podman auto-update` pulls newer images and restarts those units. Containers need a Linux kernel, so on macOS and Windows `podman machine` runs a Linux VM (libkrun by default on Macs, WSL or Hyper-V on Windows) and `podman` drives it remotely. Podman is Apache 2.0. Red Hat started it, and since January 2025 it has been a CNCF sandbox project with Buildah and Skopeo; the separate Podman Desktop GUI is also Apache 2.0 and a CNCF sandbox project.
strengths: No daemon to run or protect: containers are children of the command or systemd unit that started them, and nothing runs when no containers do
Rootless by design: an ordinary user runs containers in a user namespace, and Podman is not setuid and gains no privileges
Close to Docker: the same CLI, images and registries, plus a Docker-compatible API socket for tools such as `docker-compose`
Quadlet makes containers ordinary systemd services, with dependencies, restarts and scheduled image updates through `podman auto-update`
Pods and `podman kube play` / `podman kube generate` let you move between Kubernetes YAML and local containers
limits: Compose isn’t built in: `podman compose` hands off to an external `docker-compose` or `podman-compose`, and Docker plugins aren’t supported

Rootless networking has caveats: ports below 1024 need a sysctl change, and the default `rootlessport` forwarder hides clients’ real source IPs (a `pasta` forwarder that keeps them is experimental in 6.0)
One machine only: no Swarm and no scheduling or failover across hosts; the project points to Kubernetes for orchestration
On macOS and Windows every container runs inside a `podman machine` Linux VM, and Podman 6 dropped Intel Macs and Windows 10
Podman 6 removed cgroups v1, iptables, CNI and slirp4netns, so older hosts must be modernised or stay on the 5.8 line, which still gets releases

sections.title: Podman and Docker compared
sections.intro: Both run the same OCI images from the same registries, and most `docker` commands work unchanged with `podman`. They differ in how containers are started and supervised, and in what comes in the box.

rows.label: How containers start
values: No daemon: `podman` starts `conmon` and an OCI runtime, then exits
The `docker` client asks the `dockerd` daemon over a REST API

rows.label: Root
values: Rootful or rootless; rootless needs only subordinate UID ranges
The daemon needs root unless you opt in to Rootless mode

rows.label: Pods
values: Yes: `podman pod` shares network, IPC and hostname namespaces, like Kubernetes
No pod object; Compose groups related containers

rows.label: Keeping services running
values: Quadlet files become systemd units; `podman auto-update` refreshes images
Restart policies run by the daemon; Docker advises against process managers

rows.label: Compose
values: `podman compose` runs `docker-compose` or `podman-compose` against Podman’s socket
Docker Compose, Docker’s own tool

rows.label: Multi-host
values: None; Swarm API calls are refused
Swarm mode built into the engine

rows.label: Kubernetes YAML
values: `podman kube play` runs it; `podman kube generate` writes it
Not read by the engine; Docker Desktop includes a local Kubernetes

rows.label: Docker API
values: Compatibility layer (Docker API v1.44 in Podman 6.0) plus the Libpod API
Native

rows.label: macOS and Windows
values: `podman machine` Linux VM
Docker Desktop Linux VM (on Linux desktops too)

rows.label: Desktop app licence
values: Podman Desktop: Apache 2.0, free for everyone
Docker Desktop: proprietary; paid for companies with 250+ employees or $10 million+ revenue

rows.label: Licence and governance
values: Apache 2.0, CNCF sandbox project
Engine Apache 2.0, built from the Moby project; Docker, Inc.

notes: Docker’s Rootless mode runs the daemon itself inside a user namespace; Podman’s rootless mode has no daemon at all.

sections.title: The rest of the toolbox
sections.intro: Podman is one of several daemonless tools from the same team, sharing the same image and storage libraries.

items.name: Buildah
items.text: Builds OCI images from a `Dockerfile` or by modifying a working container, without a daemon or root. `podman build` uses it internally, and the two share image storage.

items.name: Skopeo
items.text: Copies images between registries and inspects remote images, layers included, without pulling them or running a daemon.

items.name: Podman Desktop
items.text: A GUI for Linux, macOS and Windows for working with containers, images and Kubernetes from the desktop. Free and Apache 2.0 for any size of company.

items.name: bootc
items.text: Boots and updates whole operating systems from container images, kernel included. Podman 6 uses `bootc switch` to update the OS inside `podman machine` VMs.

story: Docker starts every container as a child of one long-running daemon that normally runs as root. In 2018 Red Hat’s Dan Walsh showed what that costs: a container started through the daemon loses the login UID that Linux audit uses to record who changed a file, and systemd features such as readiness notification and socket activation can’t pass through the client/server hop. Talking to the daemon’s socket also means trusting a root process.

Podman began inside CRI-O, Red Hat’s container runtime for Kubernetes. In November 2016 engineers added `kpod` there, a client-only tool for debugging pods and images when the daemons weren’t responding, which needed no daemon itself. In November 2017 it moved to its own repository, libpod, and that December Walsh renamed it: “The decision is in, kpod is going to be named podman.” Red Hat wanted something easy for anyone used to the Docker command line that didn’t need a daemon running.

Podman 1.0 shipped in January 2019, and RHEL 8 that May dropped the Docker engine and `docker` command in favour of Podman. Later releases replaced CNI networking with Netavark, built systemd support in through Quadlet and made `pasta` the rootless network. The CNCF accepted Podman, Buildah and Skopeo as a sandbox project in January 2025, and Podman 6.0 moved them into a CNCF-owned GitHub organization.

choices.choice: Fork and exec instead of a client and a daemon
choices.why: The container is an offspring of the `podman` process, so audit keeps the real user’s login UID and systemd can pass readiness notifications and sockets straight through. When no containers run, nothing of Podman runs.

Walsh’s complaint about the daemon model was that users must open a socket to a privileged daemon. Mapping a block of subordinate UIDs into a user namespace lets an ordinary user run containers without ever holding root on the host.

Its ancestor `kpod` was a tool for inspecting and launching pods next to CRI-O, so Podman kept Kubernetes’ unit of grouped containers. That made it natural to read and write Kubernetes YAML, which `podman play kube` did by 1.0.

choices.choice: Its own network stack instead of CNI
choices.why: CNI was built for Kubernetes clusters, while Podman needed single-host features such as DNS by container name and alias. In Podman 4.0 the team replaced it with Netavark and Aardvark, written in Rust, for better IPv6, multi-network containers and speed.
